CHAIN: "Ornithine Transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency" -> "urea cycle disorder" -> "inability to convert ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Ornithine Amino Transferase deficiency" -> "gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina" -> "does not involve urea cycle directly" -> "no direct accumulation of ammonia" -> "no hyperammonemia" -> 90%
analysis: The question requires identifying which enzyme deficiency does not commonly feature hyperammonemia. Hyperammonemia is a condition characterized by elevated levels of ammonia in the blood, which is typically associated with disorders in the urea cycle. The urea cycle is a critical pathway that converts ammonia to urea, which is then excreted from the body. Deficiencies in enzymes involved in this cycle can lead to an accumulation of ammonia, resulting in hyperammonemia. Argininosuccinate synthetase, Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase (CPS-I), and Ornithine Transcarbamoylase (OTC) are all enzymes directly involved in the urea cycle. Deficiencies in any of these enzymes disrupt the cycle, leading to the accumulation of ammonia. In contrast, Ornithine Amino Transferase deficiency primarily affects the metabolism related to the eyes, specifically causing gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina, and does not interfere with the urea cycle. Therefore, it does not typically result in hyperammonemia. This analysis aligns with the standard medical understanding and consensus on the role of these enzymes in metabolic pathways.
